summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code of practice on single-sex services do not automatically extend to Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. Local law governs the territory, and those United Kingdom measures can be applied only by Order in Council, so a visitor should expect the territory's own statutes and practices rather than the United Kingdom framework to determine how single-sex services, records and complaints are handled.

Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful in the territory since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across Saint Helena, Ascension Island and Tristan da Cunha. The 2009 constitutional order imposed by the United Kingdom bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation territory-wide, and those protections have been in force since 2009.

Same-sex marriage was legislated island by island. The Ascension Island Council approved the marriage ordinance on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0; it was signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016 and commenced on 1 January 2017. Tristan da Cunha followed on 4 August 2017 and Saint Helena on 20 December 2017.

Adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2017. The territory is classified as an Overseas Country or Territory of the European Union, and the applicability of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights is recorded on that basis.
tangentialFactors:
Because the United Kingdom's 2025 single-sex-services code does not apply of its own force, provisions elsewhere in the British Islands that shape how toilets, changing rooms and shelters admit people are not a reliable guide to what a visitor will encounter on Saint Helena, Ascension or Tristan da Cunha.

Ascension Island carried the territory's marriage reform first, and by the largest margin on record for the measure, with the Ascension Island Council voting 5 to 0 on 31 May 2016. Saint Helena, the most populous island, legislated last, on 20 December 2017.

GayLawNet's account of the territory's status as an Overseas Country or Territory of the European Union and the resulting Charter applicability was accessed in June 2013 and rests on the classification as recorded at that time; the current operational reach of the Charter in the territory is not addressed in the sources reviewed.
localsOnly:
Residents are covered by the anti-discrimination clause of the 2009 constitutional order, which has been in force territory-wide since 2009 and names sexual orientation among the protected grounds.

Local councils legislate for their own islands on family law: the Ascension Island Council passed its marriage ordinance on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0, and the instrument was signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016 before commencing on 1 January 2017. Tristan da Cunha legislated on 4 August 2017 and Saint Helena on 20 December 2017.

Adoption by same-sex couples has been available to residents since 2017. Residents' access to single-sex services and to remedies for discrimination remains a matter of local law, since the United Kingdom equality statute and its codes reach the islands only through an Order in Council.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses legal gender recognition, the issue or amendment of gender markers on passports or birth certificates, or access to gender-affirming healthcare in the territory. Whether any local instrument regulates these matters is unresolved.

Hate-crime provisions, offences based on gender identity, and rules on restroom or facility access by gender are not sourced here and remain unresolved rather than absent.

The inventory documents the anti-discrimination clause in force since 2009 but contains no reported complaints, enforcement actions or case law under it, so its practical operation for a visitor is unresolved.

The Alchetron entry carries a snapshot date of 25 April 2026 and aggregates several claims; the underlying legislation is corroborated by other sources, but any change after that date is unresolved.
